prompt:
Render a clean, straight-on printed MUSIC-THEORY worksheet titled 'TWO-SYSTEM MELODY CHECK'. Show the SAME short melody written in TWO notation systems, stacked, so they line up column by column.

TOP LINE -- JIANPU (numbered notation) in the key of C major, where digit 1=C(do), 2=D, 3=E, 4=F, 5=G, 6=A, 7=B; a dot ABOVE a digit raises it one octave, a dot BELOW lowers it one octave; with no dot the pitch is in the octave starting at middle C. Print exactly these 6 numbers left to right, evenly spaced: 3, 7, 2 (dot ABOVE), 5, 1, 6. Under each number print its column index (1..6) in small red type.

BOTTOM LINE -- a five-line TREBLE STAFF with a treble clef at the left. For EACH column, draw one notehead at the staff line or space of the SAME pitch that the jianpu digit above it names (same key of C major; apply the octave dots). The two systems must AGREE note for note: the notehead in column k must sit at exactly the pitch the jianpu number in column k encodes -- so higher digits (and dots-above) go higher on the staff, lower ones go lower. Do NOT assume a default octave -- apply each digit's octave dots. Space the noteheads evenly so each lines up under its jianpu digit. Make the staff, clef and noteheads large and legible; all pitches are naturals, no sharps or flats.
easy_question: This image was supposed to depict a music-theory worksheet with TWO stacked lines: a line of jianpu numbers (numbered notation) on top and a five-line treble STAFF with noteheads below. Ignoring artistic quality, does the image actually DEPICT that -- a row of numbers above a musical staff with noteheads? A clean diagram counts as yes. Answer NO only if it shows just plain text, a blank card, or something unrelated. Answer yes or no only.
